scene.testo: The question was simple. Why did Germany, a nation that built the world's most feared air force, never build enough bombers? Allied officers put it to Field Marshal Erhard Milch, and they waited for his answer.

It was 1945. Germany had collapsed. Milch, Hermann Göring's deputy at the Air Ministry, was now a prisoner, questioned by British and American interrogators who wanted to understand how the German air war had been run.

Milch had been captured in May 1945 by British forces in northern Germany. Soon afterward, he began giving statements to Allied investigators. The officers had a stack of questions. One of them concerned the bomber.

Erhard Milch was an airline executive before he was a field marshal. He had served in the air arm in the First World War. By 1933 he was Göring's state secretary for aviation, helping build an air force in secret.

The Treaty of Versailles had banned a German air force. So early planning was hidden behind civilian aviation. In 1935, Hitler dropped the pretense, and the Luftwaffe was openly announced to the world.

Early on, a strategic bomber was part of the plan. General Walther Wever, the first Luftwaffe chief of staff, wanted aircraft that could strike deep into enemy territory. He argued for what became known as the Ural bomber.
Two prototypes were built, the Dornier Do 19 and the Junkers Ju 89. Both were large, four-engine aircraft. Neither would ever enter production. On June 3, 1936, Wever was killed in a plane crash.

After his death, the long-range bomber lost its strongest advocate. The Ural bomber program was dropped. Many historians point to this moment. But the answer Milch gave pointed elsewhere. The Luftwaffe turned to twin-engine designs.

The Spanish Civil War shaped German thinking. Fast twin-engine bombers and dive bombers, used by the Condor Legion, seemed to work. German planners concluded that tactical air power, supporting armies, was what a short war needed.

Ernst Udet, a First World War ace, was a passionate champion of the dive bomber. He headed the Technical Office of the Air Ministry from 1936 and later became director-general of equipment. His influence on aircraft design grew.

Then came the Junkers Ju 88. It first flew in December 1936 as a fast, medium-sized bomber. Early test results were promising. It looked like exactly the aircraft the Luftwaffe needed. Its speed impressed everyone who saw it.

Then the requirements changed. Officials demanded that the Ju 88 also be able to dive-bomb. Dive-bombing needs a strong airframe. Extra reinforcement, dive brakes and new fittings were added, and the weight of the aircraft kept climbing.

Delays followed. Production plans slipped. The Ju 88, once a simple, fast bomber, became a complicated machine, and the program fell far behind schedule. It did not reach the front in large numbers until after the war began.
The same logic reached the largest bomber project. The Heinkel He 177 was meant to be a heavy bomber with a long range. But it too was required to dive, and that demand shaped its entire design.

To make a dive-capable bomber with only two propellers, Heinkel's engineers coupled two engines together on each wing. The arrangement overheated. Engine fires became a notorious problem, and crews came to fear the aircraft.

The He 177 first flew in November 1939. Years of repairs and redesigns followed. Meanwhile, the Americans and British were building four-engine bombers, the B-17, the B-24, the Lancaster, without any requirement to dive.

In September 1939, war began. In 1940, the Luftwaffe went against Britain. Its medium bombers carried modest bomb loads, and its aircraft lacked the range and defensive strength to withstand a sustained air campaign.

The Battle of Britain showed the limits. German bombers suffered heavy losses over England, and the campaign did not break British resistance. Germany still had no heavy bomber force ready to continue the strategic fight.

Production numbers told the story. Through the early war years, Germany built far fewer bombers than the Allies would. Several different bomber designs competed for scarce engines, aluminum and factory space, and none was produced in sufficient quantity.
On November 17, 1941, Ernst Udet shot himself in Berlin. His office was in disarray, and the aircraft program was in crisis. Hermann Göring then turned to Milch to take over aircraft production.

Milch now saw the problems from the inside. He cut the number of aircraft types, pushed for standardization, and demanded more output from the factories. Production did rise, though it was never enough to replace what the war consumed.
In 1942, the air war began to turn against Germany. American heavy bombers joined the British, and bombs began falling on German cities day and night. The Reich now needed fighters in huge numbers.

By 1943, Milch was arguing that fighters were the priority. He believed that defense of German skies mattered more than new offensive bombers, and he pressed for more fighter production. Hitler, however, kept demanding bombers for retaliation.

In July 1943, Allied bombers devastated Hamburg. Firestorms swept the city, and tens of thousands died. The attack shook the German leadership. It also showed how little Germany could do to answer in kind.

Back in 1945, the interrogators asked Milch to explain it all. Why no heavy bomber force? Why so many delays? They could have expected a long list of causes: politics, rivalries, shortages. Instead, Milch gave them one.
The answer: a single requirement. Milch pointed to the demand that bombers be able to dive. In his account, that one decision, taken early, had crippled the designs that mattered and wasted years.

Why would a dive requirement matter so much? A dive-bomber must survive violent pullouts at high speed. That demands a heavy, rigid structure. A heavier structure cuts range, bomb load and speed, the very qualities a strategic bomber needs.
The requirement had powerful backers. Udet championed it, and Göring approved it. Engineers who doubted it had little room to object. By the time the doubts were heard, years had already been lost.

Consider what that meant in practice. The Allies built bombers to carry heavy loads over long distances. Germany ordered bombers that could also dive, and then struggled to make them fly reliably. Two air forces prepared for different wars.

The He 177 shows the cost most clearly. Great effort went into a bomber that was repeatedly grounded by fires and failures. It reached units only in small numbers, and it never became the heavy bomber Germany needed.

Milch was not blameless. As state secretary, he oversaw aircraft production during the years these decisions were made. The requirement stood while he held power. His answer, then, is also a verdict on himself.

The consequences reached the front. By 1944, American bombers flew over Germany in huge formations. Germany had few heavy bombers of its own to strike back at British airfields, American bases or Allied supply lines.

Without strategic bombers, Germany could not take the air war to Britain's factories or the Soviet Union's industry beyond the Urals. Its air force stayed bound to the battlefield, and the battlefield was shrinking.

Germany did build fighters in large numbers in 1944, under Albert Speer's production reforms. But fuel shortages and the loss of experienced pilots meant the planes could not turn the tide. The window for bombers had closed years earlier.

An American tribunal at Nuremberg convicted Milch in 1947 of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including the use of slave labor. He received a life sentence. It was later reduced, and he was released in 1954.

The question asked in 1945 still echoes. Germany did not lack skilled engineers or factories. It lacked a clear strategy for the air war it was fighting. One requirement, a bomber that must also dive, helped seal that failure.

descrizione:
Why did Germany never build enough heavy bombers in World War II? After the war, Allied interrogators put that question to Field Marshal Erhard Milch, Hermann Göring's deputy at the Air Ministry. This documentary traces the Luftwaffe's bomber programs, from the Ural bomber to the Junkers Ju 88 and the troubled Heinkel He 177.

The story centers on the requirement that bombers also be able to dive, and how it affected weight, range, bomb load and production. It also looks at Ernst Udet, the Battle of Britain, the bombing of Hamburg and the later fighter buildup under Albert Speer.

Built on Allied records, trial history and historical research, this video explains one costly decision in Luftwaffe history.
